subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Tubular Disorders and Genital Anomalies: RTA and Cryptorchidism

steps.tx: Defective tubular excretion of hydrogen ions or reabsorption of bicarbonate produces normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Presenting with failure to thrive, polyuria, and refractory rickets, **pediatric renal tubular acidosis** (RTA) exhibits hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with a normal serum anion gap. Type 1 distal RTA involves defective alpha-intercalated cell hydrogen secretion, resulting in an inappropriately high urine pH exceeding 5.5 despite severe systemic acidaemia.
steps.say: Renal tubular acidosis causes hyperchloremic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. In distal Type 1 RTA, the urine pH remains persistently above 5.5 despite systemic acidosis.

steps.tx: Autosomal recessive transport channel mutations in the thick ascending limb of Henle mimic chronic loop diuretic exposure. In infants presenting with severe polyuria and salt wasting, **pediatric Bartter syndrome** arises from genetic defects in the NKCC2 co-transporter, ROMK potassium channel, or CLCNKB chloride channel. Patients demonstrate profound hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria with early nephrocalcinosis, markedly elevated plasma renin and aldosterone, and normal blood pressure.
steps.say: Bartter syndrome mimics chronic furosemide abuse, causing severe hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and nephrocalcinosis. Blood pressure remains completely normal.

left.title: Bartter Syndrome (Loop Defect)
points: Impaired NKCC2 or ROMK channel in loop of Henle
Severe hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Marked hypercalciuria with early nephrocalcinosis
Presents in infancy with maternal polyhydramnios

right.title: Gitelman Syndrome (Distal Defect)
points: Impaired NCCT co-transporter in distal convoluted tubule
Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesaemia
Hypocalciuria (protective against stones)
Presents in older children or adolescents with muscle cramps

steps.tx: Generalized functional impairment of proximal convoluted tubular transport leads to indiscriminate urinary wasting of solutes. Clinically characterized by glycosuria with normal blood glucose, **pediatric Fanconi syndrome** produces massive urinary loss of amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, uric acid, and potassium. The resulting hypophosphataemia triggers refractory hypophosphataemic rickets and growth failure, frequently secondary to underlying infantile nephropathic cystinosis.
steps.say: Fanconi syndrome causes proximal tubular wasting of phosphate, glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate. It causes severe refractory rickets with normal blood glucose levels.

steps.tx: Insensitivity of renal medullary collecting ducts to antidiuretic hormone impairs water reabsorption despite physiological hyperosmolality. Inherited as an X-linked recessive trait due to AVPR2 vasopressin receptor mutations, **congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus** manifests in young infants with extreme polydipsia, severe polyuria, hypernatraemic dehydration, recurrent unexplained fevers, and dilute urine with osmolality below two hundred milliosmoles per kilogram.
steps.say: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus involves collecting duct insensitivity to ADH, causing hypernatremic dehydration and dilute urine. Exogenous desmopressin produces no response.

left.title: Diagnostic Testing Profile
points: Inappropriate dilute urine during dehydration
Urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg despite high serum Na
Water deprivation test shows persistent polyuria
Failure to concentrate urine following desmopressin

right.title: Paradoxical Therapy Protocol
points: Unrestricted access to free drinking water
Hydrochlorothiazide produces paradoxical volume contraction
Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandins, enhancing water uptake
Low-solute, low-sodium dietary modifications

steps.tx: Arrested embryological development of the ventral urethral folds produces abnormal ectopic positioning of the external urethral orifice. The classic triad of **congenital hypospadias in boys** includes an abnormally located ventral urethral meatus anywhere from the glans to the perineum, ventral fibrous chordee curvature, and a dorsal hooded prepuce. Neonatal circumcision is strictly contraindicated, as the prepucial skin is required for reconstructive urethroplasty.
steps.say: Hypospadias presents with a ventral urethral opening, chordee curvature, and a hooded dorsal foreskin. Circumcision is strictly contraindicated because the prepuce is needed for repair.

vis.alt: Clinical anatomical diagram displaying hypospadias classifications, ventral chordee, and hooded dorsal prepuce.
vis.caption: Anatomical features of hypospadias showing ventral displacement of the urethral meatus. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Surgical reconstruction corrects penile curvature and constructs an adequate neourethral conduit opening at the glans tip. Optimal timing for **hypospadias urethroplasty reconstruction** is between six and eighteen months of age, before the child develops conscious body image and gender identity awareness. Reconstructive steps involve orthoplasty to release chordee, tabularized incised plate (Snodgrass) urethroplasty, and glanuloplasty with foreskin reconstruction.
steps.say: Perform hypospadias repair between six and eighteen months of age. The Snodgrass tabularized incised plate urethroplasty provides excellent functional and cosmetic results.

rows: Glans or coronal sulcus on ventral side
Along the ventral midshaft of penis
At junction of penis and scrotum
Two-stage repair; rule out DSD anomalies

steps.tx: Failure of one or both testes to descend along the retroperitoneal path into the dependent scrotal sac constitutes cryptorchidism. In term male infants, **congenital undescended testis** occurs in three percent, rising to thirty percent in premature boys. The higher intra-abdominal temperature impairs normal testicular germ cell maturation, significantly increasing long-term risks of subfertility and malignant transformation into testicular seminoma.
steps.say: Undescended testis affects three percent of term and thirty percent of preterm boys. Higher temperature impairs spermatogenesis and increases future malignancy risks.

vis.alt: Clinical examination diagram illustrating milking palpation technique along the inguinal canal for cryptorchidism.
vis.caption: Milking examination technique along the inguinal canal distinguishing retractile from undescended testes. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Clinical physical examination carefully distinguishes true undescended testes from hyperactive cremasteric retractile variants. While a retractile testis can be milked gently into the scrotal base where it remains temporarily, an undescended testis retracts immediately upon release. If spontaneous descent does not occur by six months, **surgical orchidopexy for cryptorchidism** is recommended between six and twelve months of age to preserve spermatogenesis.
steps.say: Differentiate retractile from true undescended testes using warm-hand milking examination. Perform orchidopexy between six and twelve months to preserve fertility.

left.title: Retractile Testis Features
points: Exaggerated cremasteric reflex response
Can be milked fully to scrotal bottom
Remains in scrotum until cremaster re-contracts
Normal adult spermatogenesis; no surgery needed

right.title: Surgical Orchidopexy Protocol
points: Perform between 6 and 12 months of age
Mobilize spermatic cord and ligate patent processus
Anchor testis securely in dartos pouch
Enables testicular examination for malignancy surveillance
